lithium.note: Easily confused with strontium, which is very nearly the same red. If both are possible, the flame test alone will not settle it.
lithium.source: Vogel's Textbook of Qualitative Inorganic Analysis, 5th ed. — flame tests

sodium.note: Intense, persistent, and the reason flame tests need care: almost everything is contaminated with a trace of sodium, so a brief flicker of yellow means nothing. Only a strong, lasting yellow counts.
sodium.source: Vogel's Textbook of Qualitative Inorganic Analysis, 5th ed. — flame tests

potassium.note: Pale and easily lost. Sodium's yellow drowns it completely, so potassium is looked for through blue cobalt glass, which absorbs yellow and lets the lilac through.
potassium.source: Vogel's Textbook of Qualitative Inorganic Analysis, 5th ed. — flame tests

calcium.note: Duller and more orange than the crimson of lithium or strontium. This is how calcium is separated from barium and strontium after Group V has brought all three down together.
calcium.source: Vogel's Textbook of Qualitative Inorganic Analysis, 5th ed. — flame tests

strontium.note: The red of distress flares and of red fireworks. Close enough to lithium's crimson that the two are genuinely hard to tell apart by eye.
strontium.source: Vogel's Textbook of Qualitative Inorganic Analysis, 5th ed. — flame tests

barium.note: A pale yellowish green, and the only green in the alkaline earths — so within Group V it is unmistakable.
barium.source: Vogel's Textbook of Qualitative Inorganic Analysis, 5th ed. — flame tests

copper.note: A vivid blue-green, deeper and bluer than barium's apple green. It is what makes a copper pipe flare turquoise in a fire.
copper.source: Vogel's Textbook of Qualitative Inorganic Analysis, 5th ed. — flame tests
